> residence, diabetes, family history of hypertension, health insurance,
> hypertension knowledge score and distance to the facility. Continuous
> predictors were modelled as linear terms after checking for non-linearity
> with quadratic terms. Results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95%
> profile-likelihood confidence intervals; overall associations of
> categorical variables were assessed with likelihood-ratio tests.
> Discrimination was assessed with the area under the ROC curve and
> calibration with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test. Analyses used complete cases
> and were performed in R version 4.6.

```{r c5-results-values, include=FALSE}
n_dx      <- nrow(dx)
n_uptake  <- sum(dx$treatment_uptake == "Yes")
n_model   <- nobs(model_full)
fmt_or <- function(term) {
  r <- or_table[or_table$term == term, ]
  sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f", r$estimate, r$conf.low, r$conf.high)
}
p_edu <- drop1(model_full, test = "LRT")["education", "Pr(>Chi)"]
```

### A Results paragraph

The paragraph below is written with inline R code, so every number comes
straight from the model objects created above.

> Of the `r format(n_dx, big.mark = ",")` adults with diagnosed
> hypertension, `r n_uptake` (`r round(100 * n_uptake / n_dx, 1)`%) were
> receiving antihypertensive treatment; `r n_model` had complete data and
> were included in the multivariable model. After mutual adjustment,
> treatment uptake was associated with diabetes (OR
> `r fmt_or("diabetesYes")`), health insurance (OR
> `r fmt_or("health_insuranceYes")`), a family history of hypertension (OR
> `r fmt_or("family_history_htnYes")`) and urban rather than rural
> residence (OR `r fmt_or("residenceUrban")`). The odds of uptake increased
> with educational attainment (likelihood-ratio $p =
> `r round(p_edu, 3)`$; OR for tertiary versus no education
> `r fmt_or("educationTertiary")`), with age (OR per 10 years
> `r sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f", rescaled$OR[1], rescaled$lower[1], rescaled$upper[1])`)
> and with hypertension knowledge (OR per 5 points
> `r sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f", rescaled$OR[2], rescaled$lower[2], rescaled$upper[2])`).
> Men had lower odds of uptake than women (OR `r fmt_or("sexMale")`).
> Distance to the facility was associated with lower uptake in the crude
> analysis, but after adjustment (mainly for residence) the association was
> weaker and compatible with no association (OR per 5 km
> `r sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f", rescaled$OR[3], rescaled$lower[3], rescaled$upper[3])`).
> The model showed acceptable discrimination (AUC
> `r sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f", auc_val, auc_ci[1], auc_ci[3])`)
> and no evidence of poor calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow $p =
> `r round(hl_p, 2)`$).

Notice the features of this paragraph. It starts with the participants and
the number analysed. Every OR has a 95% CI, and the reference category is
clear ("urban rather than rural", "men ... than women"). Continuous
predictors are reported per meaningful increment. A multi-level variable
is summarised by its overall LR test plus the most informative comparison.
A non-significant result (distance) is reported with its estimate and
interval, not as "not significant" alone. And the wording describes
*associations*, not effects.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Over-claiming causality. This is a cross-sectional study: exposure and
outcome were measured at the same time, so we cannot tell whether, for
example, knowledge led to treatment or treatment (and the counselling that
accompanies it) led to knowledge. Words such as "effect", "impact",
"leads to", "reduces" and "determines" imply causation. Prefer "was
associated with", "had higher odds of" and "was more common among", and
discuss reverse causation and residual confounding in the Discussion
[@vonelm2007].
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Clinical interpretation"}
If these findings were real, they would point to several groups at risk of
not receiving treatment after diagnosis: men, rural residents, people
without health insurance, those with little formal education and those with
poor knowledge of hypertension. Some of these factors (insurance coverage,
knowledge) are potentially modifiable through policy and health education.
Remember, however, that the data in this book are simulated for teaching:
the results illustrate methods, not real clinical findings.
:::

### Results, interpretation and discussion

A Results section reports what was found: numbers, intervals, and neutral
wording. The interpretation of those numbers (what they mean for patients
and services), the comparison with previous studies, and the limitations
belong in the Discussion. For this analysis the limitations section would
mention the cross-sectional design (no temporal ordering), self-reported
uptake, the complete-case analysis, possible residual confounding by
unmeasured factors such as income or severity of hypertension, and the
clustering of patients within six facilities. Finally, the Discussion
should avoid the Table 2 fallacy: the adjusted ORs are mutually adjusted
associations, not a ranking of causal effects [@westreich2013].

## Reproducible reporting {#sec-reproducible}

### Why reproducibility matters

An analysis is *reproducible* if another person, given the same data and
code, obtains the same results [@peng2011]. This is a lower bar than
*replicability* (obtaining consistent results in new data), but it is
surprisingly often not met. Numbers copied by hand from the console into a
manuscript drift out of date as the analysis evolves; figures produced by
clicking through menus cannot be regenerated; and a script that runs only
on the author's computer, with files in `C:/Users/...`, cannot be checked by
anyone else. In clinical research, where results may change practice, the
ability to retrace every step from raw data to published number is part of
scientific integrity.

### Principles for a reproducible analysis

@wilson2017 describe "good enough" practices that any researcher can adopt,
and @peng2011 describes a spectrum from publication alone to fully linked
and executable code and data. For an analysis like the one in this book,
the essential practices are as follows.

- **Keep raw data read-only.** Never edit the raw file by hand. All
  cleaning is done by a script (Chapter 2) that writes a separate clean
  file, as `analysis_data.rds` was created.
- **Organise the project.** Use one folder per project, opened as an
  RStudio Project, with sub-folders such as `Data/` (raw and clean data),
  `Scripts/` (numbered analysis scripts), `Resources/` or `Output/`
  (generated tables and figures), and `Reports/` (R Markdown or Quarto
  documents).
- **Use relative paths.** Refer to files relative to the project folder
  (`"Data/analysis_data.rds"`), never with an absolute path; the
  `here` package helps when scripts live in sub-folders.
- **Script everything.** Every table and figure should be produced by code
  that is saved, not by interactive commands typed and forgotten.
- **Set the random seed.** Any analysis involving random numbers
  (bootstrapping, multiple imputation, random splits, simulation) must call
  `set.seed()` so that it gives identical results each time.
- **Record the software environment.** Report the versions of R and of
  the key packages, since results and defaults can change between
  versions.
- **Use version control** (such as Git) to keep a history of changes to
  code and text.

### Setting the seed: an example

Maximum likelihood estimation is deterministic, so `model_full` gives the
same coefficients every time. Resampling methods are not. A bootstrap
confidence interval for the AUC, for example, draws random resamples of
the patients.

```{r c5-seed}
set.seed(2026)
ci.auc(roc_obj, method = "bootstrap", boot.n = 500, progress = "none")

set.seed(2026)          # same seed, so exactly the same interval
ci.auc(roc_obj, method = "bootstrap", boot.n = 500, progress = "none")
```

Run with the same seed, the two bootstrap intervals are identical; with a
different seed (or none) they would differ slightly from run to run. Both
are close to the analytical DeLong interval computed earlier.

### From script to report: R Markdown and Quarto

The most powerful tool for reproducible reporting is the *dynamic
document*, which interleaves text and code in a single file
[@xie2015]. In an R Markdown (`.Rmd`) or Quarto (`.qmd`) document, prose
is written in Markdown and analysis code is placed in *chunks*. When the
document is rendered ("knitted"), R runs every chunk in a fresh session
and inserts the output (tables, figures and numbers) into a Word, PDF or
HTML report. This book itself was produced in this way.

A minimal analysis report has three parts:

1. A *header* (written in YAML) with the title, author, date and output
   format, for example `output: word_document` in R Markdown or
   `format: docx` in Quarto.
2. *Code chunks* that load the packages and data, fit the models and
   produce the tables and figures exactly as in this chapter.
3. *Text* with inline R code, so that numbers in sentences are computed
   rather than typed. The Results paragraph in Section 5.11 was written
   this way: an inline expression such as `nrow(dx)`, placed between
   backticks after the letter `r`, is replaced by its value
   (`r nrow(dx)`) when the document is rendered.

Because the report is regenerated from the data each time, a correction to
the cleaning script, or an updated data set, flows automatically into every
number, table and figure. There is no step at which a number can be copied
wrongly.

The code below shows how outputs would be saved from a script. In a real
project they would go to an output folder; here they are written to a
temporary directory so that nothing in the project is changed.

```{r c5-save-outputs}
out_dir <- tempdir()     # in a project: "Resources" or "Output"

# Regression table and forest plot data as CSV
write_csv(or_table, file.path(out_dir, "regression_table.csv"))

# The forest plot as a high-resolution PNG
forest_plot <- ggplot(forest_df, aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), width = 0.25,
                orientation = "y") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "forest_plot.png"), forest_plot,
       width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

list.files(out_dir, pattern = "regression_table|forest_plot")
```

### Recording the software environment

`sessionInfo()` prints the R version, the operating system and every loaded
package with its version. In a report, you would include it in an appendix
or supplementary file, for example with
`writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session_info.txt")`. The full
output is long; the essential information is shown below.

```{r c5-session}
R.version.string
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "broom", "gtsummary", "car", "pROC", "ggplot2")
tibble(package = pkgs,
       version = map_chr(pkgs, \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Good practice"}
Before submitting a paper, restart R, clear the workspace, and run (or
render) the whole analysis from the raw data to the final report in one go.
If it runs without error and reproduces every number in the manuscript,
your analysis is reproducible. If it does not, it is better that you find
out now than a reviewer later.
:::

## Summary {#sec-summary-ch5}

This chapter brought together the skills of the previous chapters to answer
the study's main question with regression models. Linear regression models
the mean of a continuous outcome as a linear function of several
predictors, estimated by least squares; its coefficients are differences in
means, holding other predictors fixed, and its assumptions are checked with
residual plots. For a binary outcome, logistic regression models the
log-odds as a linear function of the predictors, estimated by maximum
likelihood; exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios, which approximate
risk ratios only when the outcome is rare.

We fitted a pre-specified multivariable logistic regression for treatment
uptake among 992 patients with diagnosed hypertension and complete data,
read the `summary()` output line by line, converted coefficients to odds
ratios with profile-likelihood confidence intervals, rescaled continuous
predictors to meaningful increments, and tested education as a whole with a
likelihood-ratio test. Comparing crude and adjusted estimates showed that
the apparent association between distance and uptake was largely explained
by residence, a clear example of confounding, while the changes in the ORs
for family history and insurance partly reflected non-collapsibility. The model
had adequate events per variable, no collinearity, no evidence of
non-linearity or poor calibration, and acceptable discrimination. Finally,
we presented the results as a merged crude and adjusted table and a forest
plot, wrote Methods and Results paragraphs in line with STROBE, and saw how
dynamic documents, seeds and a recorded software environment make the whole
analysis reproducible.

::: {.callout-important title="Key points"}
- Decide the purpose of a model (description, prediction or explanation)
  and its predictors before looking at the outcome data.
- In logistic regression, $\exp(\beta)$ is the odds ratio for a one-unit
  increase, holding the other predictors fixed; report continuous
  predictors per clinically meaningful increment, $\exp(c\beta)$.
- Odds ratios exaggerate risk ratios when the outcome is common; say "odds",
  and add predicted probabilities or risk ratios when readers need risks.
- Report the number of patients analysed: `glm()` silently drops anyone
  with a missing value in any model variable.
- Use likelihood-ratio tests (`drop1()`, `anova(test = "LRT")`) for
  multi-level factors and for comparing nested models fitted to the same
  patients.
- A change from crude to adjusted OR may reflect confounding, but ORs are
  non-collapsible; reason causally, and do not interpret every adjusted OR
  as a causal effect (the Table 2 fallacy).
- Avoid stepwise selection in explanatory models; check events per
  variable, collinearity (VIF), linearity, discrimination (AUC),
  calibration and influential observations.
- Present crude and adjusted ORs with 95% CIs in a `gtsummary` table and a
  log-scale forest plot; write results as associations, following STROBE.
- Make the analysis reproducible: scripts, relative paths, `set.seed()`,
  dynamic documents and a record of software versions.
:::

## Further reading {#sec-further-reading-ch5}

- @hosmer2013, *Applied Logistic Regression*: the standard reference on
  logistic regression, covering model building, interpretation of odds
  ratios, goodness of fit and diagnostics in depth.
- @vittinghoff2012, *Regression Methods in Biostatistics*: a clear,
  example-driven account of linear, logistic, Poisson and Cox regression,
  with an excellent chapter on choosing predictors for different purposes.
- @harrell2015, *Regression Modeling Strategies*: the definitive guide to
  building prediction models responsibly, including the case against
  stepwise selection, splines, validation and calibration.
- @westreich2013 and @vanderweele2019: two short, readable papers on how to
  choose adjustment variables and how (not) to interpret a multivariable
  model's coefficients.
- @vonelm2007, the STROBE statement: the checklist to follow when writing up
  any observational study.

## Exercises {#sec-exercises-ch5}

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.1"}
Using the full `analysis_data` (all 1,500 adults), fit a linear regression
of systolic blood pressure (`sbp_mmhg`) on `age`, `bmi` and `sex`.

1. Report the coefficient for age per 10 years, with its 95% CI.
2. Interpret the coefficient for `sexMale` in one sentence.
3. How much of the variation in SBP does the model explain?
4. Draw the residuals-versus-fitted plot. Are the assumptions reasonable?
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.2"}
Among the diagnosed patients (`dx`), cross-tabulate `family_history_htn`
against `treatment_uptake`.

1. Calculate by hand the proportion and the odds of uptake in each group,
   and the crude odds ratio.
2. Fit `glm(treatment_uptake ~ family_history_htn, family = binomial)` and
   confirm that `exp(coef())` gives the same OR.
3. Calculate the crude risk ratio and compare it with the OR. Why do they
   differ? Check your answer with the Zhang and Yu formula.
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.3"}
From `model_full`, calculate the adjusted odds ratio and 95% CI for:

1. a 10-year increase in age;
2. a 5-point increase in knowledge score;
3. a 10 km increase in distance to the facility.

Which of these increments do you consider most clinically meaningful, and
why should the increment be chosen before the analysis?
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.4"}
Investigate whether the association between health insurance and uptake is
confounded.

1. Using the complete-case data `cc`, fit the crude model for
   `health_insurance` and compare its OR with the adjusted OR from
   `model_full`. Calculate the percentage change in the log OR.
2. Describe in words a causal diagram for insurance and uptake. Which of the
   other model variables might be confounders, and could any be mediators?
3. Is the change you observed best explained by confounding or by
   non-collapsibility? Justify your answer.
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.5"}
Education is an ordered variable.

1. Use `drop1()` to obtain the likelihood-ratio test for education in
   `model_full`, and state the null hypothesis it tests.
2. Create a numeric version of education (0 = None, 1 = Primary,
   2 = Secondary, 3 = Tertiary) and refit the model with it in place of the
   factor. Interpret the OR "per level of education".
3. Compare the two models with AIC. Which would you report, and why?
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.6"}
Patients were recruited from six facilities.

1. Add `facility` to `model_full` and test it with a likelihood-ratio test.
2. Does adding facility change any of the other adjusted ORs by more than
   10%?
3. Compare the AUC of the two models. What do you conclude about the role
   of facility in this analysis?
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.7"}
A health economist suggests that health insurance might matter more for
rural patients, who face higher costs of travel.

1. Add the interaction `health_insurance:residence` to `model_full` and test
   it with a likelihood-ratio test.
2. From the interaction model, calculate the OR for insurance separately in
   rural and in urban patients.
3. Write two sentences reporting the result, as you would in a paper.
:::

::: {.exercise title="Exercise 5.8"}
A secondary outcome is blood pressure control (`bp_controlled`), defined
only among patients on treatment.

1. Restrict the data to diagnosed patients with `treatment_uptake == "Yes"`
   and tabulate `bp_controlled`. How many events are there?
2. Using the 10 events-per-variable guideline, how many parameters can a
   logistic model for BP control support?
3. Pre-specify and fit a model with no more than that number of parameters
   (for example age, sex, BMI and adherence). Report the adjusted ORs with
   95% CIs and the AUC.
4. Write a short Results paragraph (about 100 words) that reports the
   findings appropriately, including the limitations imposed by the small
   number of events.
:::
